“I then reasoned backward from the evidence. The murderers had escaped through one of these windows. If so, they could not have fastened the windows from inside afterward, as they were found fastened. This apparently obvious objection had brought the police investigation of the windows to a halt. Yet they were fastened. They must therefore be capable of fastening themselves. There was no avoiding that conclusion. I went to the unobstructed window, pulled out the nail with some difficulty, and tried to lift the sash. As I had expected, it resisted every effort. I now knew there must be a concealed spring, and this confirmation convinced me that my initial reasoning, at least, was sound, however mysterious the nails remained. A careful search soon revealed the hidden spring. I pressed it and, satisfied with what I had discovered, left the sash down.

“I then put the nail back and examined it closely. Anyone climbing out through this window could have shut it afterward, allowing the spring to catch, but could not have replaced the nail. The conclusion was clear and narrowed my investigation further. The murderers must have escaped through the other window. Assuming the springs on both windows were alike, as seemed probable, there must be some difference between the nails, or at least in the way they were fitted. Climbing onto the bed's fabric support, I examined the second window closely over the headboard. I slid my hand down behind the board and easily found and pressed the spring. As I had supposed, it worked exactly like the other. I then inspected the nail. It was just as thick as its counterpart and apparently fitted in the same way, driven in almost to its head.

“You will say I was baffled; but if you think that, you have misunderstood the reasoning. To borrow a phrase from hunting, I had never once lost the trail. Not for an instant had I lost the scent. Every link in the chain was sound. I had followed the mystery to its final point, and that point was the nail. As I say, in every respect it looked identical to the nail in the other window. But however conclusive that resemblance might appear, it counted for absolutely nothing beside the fact that the trail ended here, at precisely this spot. ‘There must be something wrong with the nail,’ I told myself. I touched it, and the head, together with about a quarter of an inch of the shaft, came away in my fingers.

Directly before him, in the pale moonlight, stood an old man of terrifying appearance. His eyes glowed like burning red coals; long gray hair hung in tangled coils over his shoulders. His clothes, cut in an ancient fashion, were dirty and torn, and heavy iron cuffs and rusty shackles hung from his wrists and ankles.

“Dear sir,” said Mr. Otis, “I really must insist that you oil those chains. For that purpose, I've brought you a small bottle of Tammany Rising Sun Lubricator. I understand that a single application is completely effective, and the wrapper carries several statements confirming this from some of our country's most distinguished clergymen. I'll leave it here beside the bedroom candles, and will be delighted to provide more if you need it.” Having said this, the United States Minister placed the bottle on a marble table, closed his door, and went back to bed.

For a moment the Canterville ghost stood perfectly still in understandable indignation. Then he hurled the bottle onto the polished floor and fled along the corridor, groaning hollowly and giving off an eerie green light. Just as he reached the top of the great oak staircase, however, a door flew open. Two small figures in white nightclothes appeared, and a large pillow whistled past his head! Clearly there was no time to waste. Hastily choosing the Fourth Dimension of Space as his escape route, he disappeared through the wood paneling, and the house fell completely silent.

When he reached a small hidden room in the left wing, he leaned against a moonbeam to catch his breath and tried to make sense of his situation. Never in an illustrious, uninterrupted career of three hundred years had anyone insulted him so outrageously. He thought of the Dowager Duchess, whom he had frightened into a fit while she stood at her mirror in lace and diamonds; of the four housemaids who had become hysterical when he merely grinned at them from behind the curtains in a spare bedroom; of the parish rector, whose candle he had blown out as the man left the library late one night, and who had remained under Sir William Gull's care ever since, suffering dreadfully from nervous disorders. And he thought of old Madame de Tremouillac, who had woken early one morning to find a skeleton sitting in an armchair beside the fire, reading her diary. She had spent six weeks in bed with brain fever, and after recovering had returned to the Church and severed her association with that notorious skeptic, Monsieur de Voltaire.

She would make so charming a companion for Emma.”

Mr. Woodhouse assented to everything, but observed,

“Our little friend Harriet Smith, though, is quite as pretty a sort of young person. You will be pleased with Harriet. Emma could wish for no better companion than Harriet.”

“I am exceedingly glad to hear it—only Jane Fairfax is known to be so remarkably accomplished and superior!—and precisely of Emma's age.”

The subject was pursued with great satisfaction, and others of equal importance followed and were dismissed with equal agreement; yet the evening was not to end without a slight renewal of uneasiness. The arrival of the gruel furnished abundant conversation—praise and observations in plenty—absolute certainty of its benefit to every constitution, and rather fierce denunciations of the many houses in which it was never served tolerably. Unfortunately, among the examples of failure the daughter could supply, the latest, and therefore the most memorable, concerned her own cook at South End. This young woman, engaged for their stay, had never understood what was intended by a basin of agreeable, smooth gruel, thin, yet not excessively thin. However often it had been desired and ordered, nothing acceptable had ever appeared. This offered a perilous opening.

“Ah!” said Mr. Woodhouse, shaking his head and regarding her with affectionate anxiety. To Emma's ear the exclamation meant, “Ah! the melancholy results of your journey to South End are endless. One cannot bear to speak of it.” For a little while she hoped he would indeed leave it unspoken, and that quiet reflection would be enough to recover his enjoyment of his own smooth gruel. After several minutes, however, he began,

“I shall never cease regretting that you went to the seaside this autumn instead of visiting us.”

“But why regret it, sir? I assure you, the children benefited greatly.”

“And besides, if you had to visit the sea, South End ought not to have been your choice. It is an unhealthy place. Perry was astonished to learn that you had settled on South End.”

“I know a great many people think so, but they are truly mistaken, sir. We were all in excellent health there, and never suffered the smallest inconvenience from the mud. Mr. Wingfield says that the notion of its being unhealthy is altogether wrong; and I am certain his judgment is trustworthy, for he understands the character of the air thoroughly, and his own brother and family have visited repeatedly.”

“If you were to go anywhere, my dear, it should have been Cromer. Perry once spent a week at Cromer, and considers it the finest of all places for sea-bathing.
